sections.h: Daniel 7:13-14: one like a son of man
sections.b: In Daniel's night vision, after four beasts from the sea, a figure who looks human comes with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days and is given an everlasting kingdom over all peoples (Daniel 7:13-14). The Aramaic is kevar enash, 'like a human being'. Many scholars take it as a description, not yet a title; Christian readers, from Mark 14:62 and Revelation 1:13 on, read the figure as already the Christ. The angel who explains the vision speaks only of 'the holy ones of the Most High' receiving the kingdom (7:18, 22, 27), so readers have taken the figure as the Messiah (Rashi, Sanhedrin 98a), an angel such as Michael (Collins) or Gabriel, a second divine figure (Boyarin), or a symbol of the faithful people of Israel (Noth, Casey, N. T. Wright). Whether the medieval Jewish commentator Ibn Ezra read the figure as Israel or as the Messiah is reported both ways in the secondary sources. The Old Greek has the figure coming 'on the clouds' and appearing 'like an ancient of days', not coming to him. The Gospels have Jesus apply the picture to himself before the high priest (Mark 14:62; Matthew 26:64), and Revelation 1:13 and 14:14 call the figure 'like a son of man' in the same lower-case phrase.
sections.refs: Daniel 7:13-14; Daniel 7:18, 22, 27; Mark 14:62; Matthew 26:64; Revelation 1:13; Revelation 14:14

common: Many scholars, and the Gospels' own usage (Mark 14:62), link the title 'the Son of Man' to Daniel 7:13; Casey argues that the Gospel phrase is an ordinary Aramaic idiom for 'a man', and others derive it from 1 Enoch 46-71.
uncommon: The figure is a collective symbol of the faithful Jewish people and Jesus used the phrase of himself as their representative (N. T. Wright), or as an ordinary Aramaic idiom for 'a man like me' (Casey).

sections.h: The Ancient of Days in Daniel 7
sections.b: Daniel 7:9, 13 and 22 call God attiq yomin, 'one advanced in days', an old and wise judge in white, sitting on a throne of flames whose wheels are blazing fire, with a stream of fire pouring from him and countless servants before him. The picture draws on Ezekiel 1 and on older Near Eastern pictures of the aged high god (El is called 'father of years' at Ugarit, a parallel proposed by Emerton, Day and others). 1 Enoch 46:1, a work held as Scripture by the Ethiopian church, has 'one who had a head of days' beside a son of man. The Plain English Translation keeps the title 'the Ancient of Days'. Revelation 1:14 gives the risen Christ the white hair of the Ancient of Days, and some Christian readers have taken this to say that Christ shares God's identity, while others hold that the Ancient of Days is the Father alone.
sections.refs: Daniel 7:9-10; Daniel 7:13; Daniel 7:22; Ezekiel 1:26-28; 1 Enoch 46:1; Revelation 1:13-14

sections.h: Daniel 7:25: a time, times and half a time
sections.b: The first of Daniel's time-periods that Revelation takes up. The little horn speaks against the Most High, wears down the holy ones and tries to change the appointed times and the law, and these are given into his hand for 'a time, times and half a time' (Daniel 7:25). The Aramaic is iddan veiddanin ufelag iddan, one period, two periods and half a period. In the Maccabean reading it is the three-odd years from the profaning of the temple in December 167 BC to its rededication in December 164 (1 Maccabees 1:54; 4:52). Historicists count 1,260 years; dispensationalists, three and a half years in a future tribulation. Rashi calls the end 'obscure'.
sections.refs: Daniel 7:25; Daniel 12:7; Daniel 9:27; Revelation 12:14; Revelation 11:2-3; 1 Maccabees 1:54; 1 Maccabees 4:52

sections.h: The four beasts of Daniel 7 and the beast of Revelation
sections.b: Four beasts climb out of the great sea in Daniel 7: a lion with eagle's wings, a bear raised on one side with three ribs in its mouth, a leopard with four wings and four heads, and a terrifying fourth beast with iron teeth and ten horns. The angel calls them four kings (7:17) and four kingdoms (7:23). Revelation 13:1-2 gathers all four into a single beast from the sea with ten horns and seven heads, 'like a leopard', with feet like a bear's and a mouth like a lion's, and Revelation 17:12 explains the horns as ten kings. Readers divide on whether Daniel's beasts are Babylon, Media, Persia and Greece or Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome.

sections.h: Daniel 4: the king who was humbled
sections.b: Daniel 4 is written as Nebuchadnezzar's own letter. He dreams of a great tree cut down, Daniel explains that it is the king, and the Most High drives him out from among people to live like an animal for seven periods, until he learns that the Most High is ruler over the kingdom of humankind. The sentence falls as he boasts over Babylon (4:30), and when his reason returns he blesses the King of heaven. No Babylonian text records such an illness. A Qumran Aramaic prayer (the Prayer of Nabonidus, 4Q242) tells of a similar seven years for the last king, Nabonidus, and many scholars see the story as passing from one king to the other. The Old Greek of the chapter is very different.

sections.h: Belshazzar in Daniel 5
sections.b: Daniel 5 shows King Belshazzar drinking from the temple's vessels at a banquet when a hand writes on the wall; he is killed that night. Babylonian records know him as Bel-shar-usur, eldest son and crown prince of Nabonidus, who held the army and the government in Babylon while his father was away at Teima in Arabia for about ten years. No Babylonian text calls him king, and Daniel's description of him as son of Nebuchadnezzar is debated. His story also frames chapter 7, dated to his first year.

sections.h: Daniel 5:31-6:28: Darius the Mede
sections.b: 'Darius the Mede' receives the kingdom of Babylon at about sixty-two (Daniel 5:31), appoints 120 satraps and signs the ban that sends Daniel to the lions (6:1-28), and reigns in 'the first year' of Daniel 9:1 and 11:1. No text outside Daniel names him. The chief answers are: the Persian general Gubaru or Ugbaru who took Babylon (Whitcomb); Cyrus under another name (Wiseman); the Median king Cyaxares or Astyages; or a figure built from Darius I of Persia and the idea of a Median kingdom between Babylon and Persia (Rowley, Collins). The Old Greek calls him 'Artaxerxes the Mede'.
sections.refs: Daniel 5:31; Daniel 6:1, 9, 25, 28; Daniel 9:1; Daniel 11:1; Isaiah 13:17; Jeremiah 51:11, 28

sections.h: Daniel 4-5: Babylon proud and fallen
sections.b: In Daniel, Babylon is the city Nebuchadnezzar boasts of building (4:30) and the city that falls in one night while Belshazzar feasts (5:30). The first is a mark of the king's pride, the second the end of the kingdom, 'counted out and finished'. Babylonian sources confirm the building and, in the Nabonidus Chronicle, the capture without battle in October 539 BC. The lion with eagle's wings of Daniel 7:4 is Babylon. Revelation 14:8 and 18:2 take up the title 'Babylon the Great' for the final proud city.
sections.refs: Daniel 4:30; Daniel 5:30; Daniel 7:4; Isaiah 13-14; Jeremiah 50-51; Revelation 14:8; Revelation 18:2

sections.h: Daniel 6: the satraps and the law of the Medes and Persians
sections.b: Daniel 6 gives a picture of Persian rule: a king who appoints satraps and overseers (a Persian word, achashdarpan), signs decrees that cannot be undone, and seals a den with his signet ring. The phrase 'the law of the Medes and Persians' puts Media first, as in 5:28, which on the critical reading fits the book's scheme in which a Median kingdom comes between Babylon and Persia. Esther 1:19 and 8:8 also tell of irrevocable decrees. Persian kings were known for tolerating the gods of their subjects; no outside record shows a ban like Darius's.

sections.h: Daniel 6:28: in the reign of Cyrus
sections.b: The last verse of the Aramaic court tales says that Daniel 'prospered during the reign of Darius and during the reign of Cyrus the Persian' (6:28). The Aramaic 'and' could also mean 'that is', as D. J. Wiseman argued, which would make Darius the Mede another name for Cyrus. Daniel's last vision is dated to Cyrus's third year (10:1).

sections.h: Daniel 2:4-7:28: the Aramaic of Daniel
sections.b: Daniel 2:4b-7:28 is written in Aramaic, the rest in Hebrew. The Aramaic chapters (the four-kingdom dream, the furnace, the tree, the feast, the lions' den and the beasts) form a chiasm. Persian loanwords such as raz 'secret' (4:9), dat 'law' (6:5) and achashdarpan 'satrap' (6:1) appear. Whether the language is close to the Official Aramaic of the Persian empire (sixth to fifth century) or to later Aramaic is part of the debate over the book's date. The Qumran copies of these chapters (4QDan-a, -b and -d) are in Aramaic.

sections.h: Daniel 7: the little horn
sections.b: A small horn comes up among the ten horns of the fourth beast, uproots three, and has eyes like a human's eyes and a mouth speaking big words (Daniel 7:8, 20). The angel says he will speak against the Most High, wear down the holy ones and try to change the times and the law for a time, times and half a time (7:25). Readers identify him as Antiochus IV (the critical majority), Titus (Rashi), the future Antichrist (Hippolytus, Jerome, Cyril of Jerusalem, Catholic and dispensationalist futurists), the papacy (historicists), or a Roman emperor (preterists). Later Christian writing on the Antichrist drew on this chapter along with Daniel 8 and 11 and 2 Thessalonians 2.

sections.h: Daniel 7: the first apocalypse in the book
sections.b: Daniel 7 has the marks of an apocalypse: a dream vision, symbolic beasts from the sea, a scene in heaven, an interpreting angel, and a final kingdom of God that follows the judgment of the beasts. Scholars (John Collins) see it as an early example of the kind of writing that flowered in 1 Enoch, 4 Ezra and Revelation. The first half of the book (chapters 1-6) is told about Daniel; from chapter 7 he tells his own visions and needs an angel to explain them.
sections.refs: Daniel 7:1-28; Daniel 8:15-26; 1 Enoch 14; 1 Enoch 46-48; 4 Ezra 13; Revelation 4-5

sections.h: Daniel: the kingdom that does not pass away
sections.b: A phrase runs through Daniel's Aramaic chapters: God's kingdom is an everlasting kingdom. Nebuchadnezzar says it twice (4:3, 34), Darius once (6:26), the stone becomes a mountain (2:44), and in the vision of chapter 7 it is given to one like a son of man (7:14) and to the people of the holy ones of the Most High (7:27). Mark 1:15 and the Gospels' 'kingdom of God' draw on this language, and the Lord's Prayer's 'Your kingdom come' joins it.

sections.h: Daniel 7:9: thrones and a throne of fire
sections.b: In Daniel's court scene thrones are set in place and the Ancient of Days sits on a throne of flames with wheels of blazing fire (7:9). The wheels recall Ezekiel 1 and 10, and the plural 'thrones' has been read as seats for the heavenly court, for God and the Messiah (Rabbi Akiva), or for judging the nations and for charity toward Israel (Rashi; the Talmud's other pairing is judgment and righteousness). Revelation 4 and 20:4 rebuild the scene, with elders on thrones and thrones for those who judge.

sections.h: Daniel 7:10: the books of judgment
sections.b: In Daniel's court scene the court sits and 'the books were opened' (7:10). They are heavenly records of deeds, to be distinguished from the book of life of Daniel 12:1. Revelation 20:12 uses the same words for the last judgment and adds the book of life.

sections.h: Daniel 4 and 7: dreams that need an interpreter
sections.b: Nebuchadnezzar's dream of the tree (Daniel 4) and Daniel's dream of the four beasts (Daniel 7) are the two long dream reports of the Aramaic chapters. In chapter 4 Daniel interprets for the king, with God's help, after the Babylonian experts fail. In chapter 7 Daniel is the dreamer and needs an angel to interpret. This shift marks the move from the court tales to the visions.

sections.h: Daniel 6:10: praying toward Jerusalem three times a day
sections.b: Daniel prays three times a day, kneeling, with the windows of his upstairs room open toward Jerusalem. This follows Solomon's temple prayer, which asked God to hear those who pray toward the city from a land of exile (1 Kings 8:48-49), and Psalm 55:17. It became the pattern for Jewish daily prayer and was taken up in the Didache's three daily prayers. The ban on prayer to anyone but the king is the test.

sections.h: Daniel 4:27: righteousness and mercy to the poor
sections.b: Daniel advises Nebuchadnezzar to break with his sins by doing what is right and being kind to the poor. The Aramaic tsidqah, 'righteousness', became 'alms' in the Old Greek, in Theodotion and in Jerome's Vulgate, which made the verse a standard text for the Christian teaching that almsgiving helps to blot out sin (compare Tobit 12:9). Rashi, following the Tanhuma, reads the king's boast in 4:30 as the moment he stopped feeding the poor.

sections.h: Daniel 6: a ban on petitioning anyone but the king
sections.b: The officials' ban in Daniel 6 forbids any request of a god or person other than King Darius for thirty days. No known Persian rule did this, and critical scholars read it as an echo of ruler cults in the Greek period and of Antiochus IV's decrees. Daniel's refusal is the test of whom he serves.

sections.h: Daniel 4:17 and 7:9-10: the court of heaven
sections.b: The 'decree of the watchers' and 'word of the holy ones' in Daniel 4:17 show heaven acting as a court that carries out the Most High's sentence. In Daniel 7:9-10 the court sits with a countless host, thrones and books. The holy ones of 7:18, 22 and 27 may be the same heavenly beings, or the faithful people they protect.

sections.h: Daniel 4:13, 6:22 and 7:16: watchers and angels
sections.b: Chapters 4-7 show angels as the 'watcher, holy one' who announces Nebuchadnezzar's sentence (4:13, 17, 23), as the angel who shuts the lions' mouths (6:22), and as the one among those standing by who explains the vision (7:16). In 7:10 a thousand thousands serve the Ancient of Days.

sections.h: Daniel 5:4 and 5:23: gods of gold and silver
sections.b: Belshazzar and his nobles praise gods of gold and silver, bronze, iron, wood and stone, and Daniel charges them with honoring gods that cannot see, hear or know, while refusing the God who holds their breath in his hand (5:23). The mockery follows Isaiah 44 and Psalm 115.

sections.h: Daniel 5:2-3: the temple's vessels at Babylon's banquet
sections.b: The gold and silver vessels from the temple at Jerusalem, kept in Babylon since 597 and 586 BC, are used at Belshazzar's banquet, and he is killed that night. Cyrus returned 5,400 of them in 538 BC (Ezra 1:7-11). Under Antiochus IV the temple was robbed again of its vessels (1 Maccabees 1:21-24).

sections.h: Daniel 6: rescue for the faithful
sections.b: Daniel in the lions' den, like his three friends in the furnace, is the Bible's picture of a faithful person condemned for obeying God and saved by an angel. Hebrews 11:33-34 counts it among acts of faith, 1 Maccabees 2:60 recalls it in the speech of the dying Mattathias, and early Christian art shows Daniel among the lions as a sign of rescue from death.

sections.h: Daniel 4-7: Old Greek and Theodotion
sections.b: The Old Greek of Daniel 4-6 differs from the Aramaic as no other Old Testament text does. It dates chapter 4 to Nebuchadnezzar's eighteenth year, changes the feast in chapter 5 into the dedication of his palace, leaves out Daniel's recital of Nebuchadnezzar's fall (5:18-22), tells the story of chapter 6 with two plotters, and in 7:13 has the one like a son of man come 'on the clouds' (Theodotion and the Aramaic say 'with', the difference between Matthew 26:64 and Mark 14:62) and appear 'like an ancient of days'. The church replaced it with Theodotion's revision, which follows the Aramaic. The Old Greek survives in Codex Chisianus and in Papyrus 967.

sections.h: Daniel in the Aramaic stories and the first vision
sections.b: In chapters 4-7 Daniel is the interpreter who tells the king what his dream means (4), reads the writing on the wall (5), survives the lions' den (6) and then, in his own dream, sees four beasts and one like a son of man (7). His Babylonian name is Belteshazzar (4:8; 5:12), and the queen, Belshazzar and Darius call him Daniel. The Aramaic part of the book ends at 7:28.

sections.h: Daniel 7: the beasts from the sea
sections.b: Chapter 7 gives the same four kingdoms in a second image: a lion with eagle's wings, a bear raised on one side, a leopard with four wings and four heads, and a fourth beast with iron teeth and ten horns. The angel calls them four kings (7:17) and the fourth a fourth kingdom (7:23). In the scheme Babylon, Media, Persia, Greece the bear is Media and the leopard Persia, and the fourth beast and its horns are the Greek-Seleucid kingdom and Antiochus IV. In the scheme Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome the leopard is Greece (its four heads the four successors of Alexander) and the fourth beast is Rome (Rashi, Hippolytus, Jerome). The rabbinic midrash Leviticus Rabbah 13:5, reading Daniel 7, has a third scheme of its own: Babylon, Media, Greece and Edom (Rome), without Persia. In every scheme, the beasts are judged by the court of the Ancient of Days and the kingdom is given to the holy ones of the Most High (7:9-14, 26-27).
